title: MIAM: Modality Imbalance-Aware Masking for Multimodal Ecological Applications
one_liner: Train multimodal ecological models by masking inputs dynamically and more often hiding dominant modalities, so weaker modalities get enough learning pressure and the model stays usable when data is missing.
lead: Ecological prediction often combines satellite imagery, environmental time series, tabular site descriptors, and sometimes sound recordings. In practice, some sources are missing and some sources dominate training because they are easier or more predictive. A model can then lean too hard on the dominant modality and under-train the rest. MIAM addresses both problems with dynamic masking. During training, it deliberately removes different subsets of inputs, explores many cross-modality combinations, and increases masking probability on modalities that are currently dominating. The goal is not only resilience to missing data. The goal is balanced learning, so each modality becomes useful instead of being ignored.

problem.h2: Why static masking does not solve missing data or modality dominance
paras: Many multimodal training pipelines use random masking: with fixed probabilities, they drop some inputs so the model learns not to depend on one complete bundle, because it repeatedly sees partial input sets during training. That helps a little with missing data, but it does not react to which modalities are currently dominating learning because the drop pattern never changes in response to model behavior. If satellite imagery is already much stronger than a short environmental time series, a static rule may still expose imagery most of the time, so the model keeps improving the strong modality while the weak modality remains underused because the loss is still easiest to reduce through the strong source.

Ecological data also has a combinatorial structure. Missingness can happen across modalities, such as no image because of cloud cover, and within a modality, such as gaps in a time series. A static scheme explores only a small part of these combinations. That means the model is not forced to practice the hard but realistic input patterns it will face at deployment.

callout.html: Sample many more input subsets, rank them by informativeness and difficulty, and mask dominant modalities more often when their learning progress pulls far ahead.

panels.title: 1. Ecological inputs arrive unevenly
panels.caption: Some examples have all sources. Others are missing one or more of them.

panels.title: 2. One modality starts to dominate
panels.caption: The model leans on the strongest source because it reduces loss fastest.

panels.caption: The training loop reacts to current performance, not only to a fixed masking table.

steps.text: Construct many possible input combinations across and within modalities rather than relying on one fixed masking pattern.
Estimate which subsets are informative or challenging because those subsets reveal where the model still depends too much on a small set of sources.
Track relative performance and learning dynamics for each modality so the training loop can tell which source is pulling too far ahead.

steps.b: Raise masking probability on dominant modalities
steps.text: Hide strong modalities more often, which forces the model to improve the weaker ones because the training loss can no longer be reduced by relying on the dominant source again.
Inspect which variables, time segments, image regions, or sounds still drive predictions once the model has been trained under balanced masking.

paras: The paper changes the masking scheduler during training. Instead of a static drop pattern, it uses a dynamic policy that depends on how informative a subset is and how imbalanced the current modality learning has become.
object.object: Adaptive masking schedule driven by modality imbalance

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: effective modality contribution
hidden.name: How much each modality actually changes the prediction after training
paras: A multimodal model may accept many input types while only truly using one or two of them. The hidden quantity is effective contribution: if you remove one modality, how much does the prediction or confidence change, and does that change reflect genuine complementary information or only redundancy?

MIAM targets this quantity indirectly through training pressure. When one modality becomes dominant, its masking probability rises. That matters because the loss can only be reduced by extracting more value from the remaining modalities. Over time, the effective contribution profile becomes flatter: weaker modalities start to matter more, and dominant modalities matter slightly less in relative terms.

heat.caption: Darker means that factor has more influence on whether a modality truly contributes rather than merely being present.

reads.html: The model should keep working when one input source is missing because several sources should matter, not just the easiest one.
MIAM uses relative performance and learning dynamics to adapt masking toward dominant modalities, which increases balanced contribution across and within modalities.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: remove the easy shortcut while practicing realistic missingness
paras: The method works because gradient-based training, which means updating the model's internal numbers in the direction that lowers loss, will usually follow the easiest route to lower loss. If one modality, such as satellite imagery, already explains much of the target, the model can keep allocating more capacity to that modality and largely ignore weaker sources. Dynamic masking interrupts that shortcut. By hiding the dominant source more often, MIAM changes the optimization path so that the remaining modalities must carry prediction load.

The subset scoring matters because not all missingness patterns teach the same lesson. Some subsets are easy and add little new pressure. Others are hard but realistic, such as a cloudy image combined with partial weather records. Prioritizing informative or challenging subsets means training spends more time on cases that expose brittle dependence. That improves resilience under missing inputs because the model repeatedly sees the exact combinations that would otherwise produce failures at test time.

The within-modality masking angle also matters. A time series with missing intervals is not equivalent to a fully absent time series. By masking segments, MIAM teaches the model to reason from partial trajectories rather than only from complete ones. This gives the ecological model a smoother degradation pattern because it learns to use whatever fragments remain.

stages.s: Multimodal ecological record with possible missing parts
Sample a candidate subset of available inputs
Measure which modalities are dominating learning
Increase masking on dominant sources and revisit hard subsets
Balanced model that degrades gracefully when inputs go missing

math.words: The masking probability for each modality rises with its dominance score. A modality that is already strong is hidden more often so weaker modalities receive more training pressure.
symbols: default masking level for that modality
how far that modality's performance or learning speed is ahead of others

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose imagery has dominance 0.5, time series has 0.2, and tabular data has 0.1.
If the base mask rate is 0.2 for all modalities and gamma is 0.4, then imagery gets mask rate 0.2 + 0.4 times 0.5 = 0.4.
Time series gets 0.28 and tabular data gets 0.24.
The strong imagery stream is hidden more often, so the model must lower loss by learning from the weaker streams.

math.note: The paper uses a richer dynamic policy, but this equation captures the balancing principle that drives MIAM.

bars.h2: What changes relative to static masking

charts.title: Static masking
charts.note: The model works when its favorite modality is present, but performance drops sharply when that modality is missing because the other modalities stayed under-trained.

charts.title: MIAM dynamic masking
charts.note: Resilience improves because training repeatedly removes dominant signals and revisits hard subsets, which forces useful learning in the weaker streams.

items.b: The scheduler can over-mask a genuinely indispensable modality.
items.html: If one modality carries unique information that no other modality can replace, hiding it too aggressively can lower overall performance because the model is asked to infer targets from missing evidence.

items.b: Dominance estimates can be noisy early in training.
items.html: When the model is still unstable, short-term loss changes may not reflect true modality strength. Reacting too strongly at that stage can create oscillating mask rates.

items.b: Subset exploration can become too large.
items.html: The space of cross-modality and within-modality masks grows quickly. If sampling is not managed well, training can spend too much time on low-value subsets and not enough on the important ones.
Warm up with conservative mask updates, cap the maximum mask rate, and prioritize subsets whose difficulty and realism are validated on held-out data.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a multimodal ecological classifier or regressor with at least three sources, such as imagery, weather time series, and tabular site variables. Compare a no-masking baseline, a static masking baseline, and MIAM. Evaluate on full-input cases and on deployment-like cases where one source is fully missing or one source is partially corrupted.

The key measurement is not only average accuracy. It is the drop under missingness and the contribution profile after training. The paper's claim holds if MIAM keeps full-input performance steady or higher while reducing the performance collapse under missing data, because that would show the model really learned to use more than its favorite modality.
demo.metric_eq: robustness_drop = score_full - score_missing; balance_gain = contribution_balance_miam - contribution_balance_static
demo.closing: A good demo should also visualize which image regions, time segments, and variables drive the prediction, because balanced learning should show up in those contribution maps.
